description:
They are the only non-primate mammal known to have true fingerprints, complete with the same loops and whorls found on human hands. Biological anthropologist Maciej Henneberg noticed it whilst working with koalas at a wildlife park near Adelaide in the mid-1990s.

a biological anthropologist at the University of Adelaide, examined koala fingertip ridges closely enough to conclude that even careful analysis under a microscope could struggle to tell them apart from a human's.

He told The Independent in 1996 that officers should at least be aware a koala print could resemble a human one. He was equally clear that finding one at an actual crime scene would be extremely unlikely.

The popular version of this story, that koala prints have genuinely confused real detectives, does not check out. Fact-checkers have found no documented case of a koala print contaminating an investigation or a suspect being wrongly implicated. The genuine fingerprint similarity got exaggerated into a crime-solving myth.

Koalas and humans do not get their nearly identical fingerprints from a shared ancestor who had them. Evolution appears to have built the same solution twice, in two completely unrelated animals reaching for a better grip.

Sources:
- https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/article/koala-fingerprints/: reports that koalas are the only non-primate mammal known to have true fingerprints, that University of Adelaide biological anthropologist Maciej Henneberg found koala ridge patterns of loops and whorls so similar to human fingerprints that they can be difficult to distinguish even under microscopic analysis, and that Henneberg's 1996 warning to police was precautionary rather than a report of an actual mix-up.
- https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/koala-fingerprints-crime-scene/: fact-checks the popular claim that koala prints have genuinely confused real crime scene investigators, finding no documented case of a koala print contaminating an investigation, a suspect being wrongly implicated, or a case being reopened because of an animal print, and rating the crime-solving version of the story a myth built on a real, narrower finding.
